title.value: 4.4 Special warnings and precautions for use

display.value: 4.4 Special warnings and precautions for use

div.p: Hyperkalaemia has been observed in patients treated with tavorenone (see section 4.8). Risk factors for hyperkalaemia include low eGFR, higher baseline serum potassium, previous episodes of hyperkalaemia, diabetes mellitus and older age. More frequent monitoring should be considered in these patients.

Serum potassium and eGFR must be measured before initiation, 4 weeks after initiation, re-start or dose increase, and periodically thereafter (see section 4.2). If serum potassium is > 5.5 mmol/L, tavorenone must be withheld and local guidelines for the management of hyperkalaemia followed.

title.value: Concomitant use of medicinal products that increase serum potassium

div.p: The risk of hyperkalaemia may increase with concomitant medicinal products that raise serum potassium (see section 4.5). Tavorenone should not be given together with potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. amiloride, triamterene) or other mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (e.g. spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone). Tavorenone should be used with caution, and serum potassium monitored, in patients taking potassium supplements, potassium-containing salt substitutes, trimethoprim or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Temporary interruption of tavorenone may be necessary during trimethoprim treatment.

Most patients in the clinical studies were also receiving an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB). Serum potassium should be monitored when these agents are started or their dose is changed.

An initial decrease in eGFR, usually within the first 4 weeks, has been observed with tavorenone. It was mostly reversible on continued treatment or after discontinuation (see section 4.8). Renal function should be monitored periodically. If eGFR decreases by 40% or more compared with baseline, interrupting tavorenone should be considered and other causes investigated.

The risk of hyperkalaemia increases as renal function declines. Tavorenone should not be initiated in patients with eGFR < 25 mL/min/1.73 m² and should be discontinued in patients with end-stage renal disease (eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m²), because clinical data are limited (see sections 4.2 and 5.2).

Tavorenone exposure is increased in patients with moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B). The dose should not exceed 12.5 mg once daily, and additional serum potassium monitoring should be considered (see sections 4.2 and 5.2). Tavorenone is contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment (see section 4.3).

Tavorenone lowers blood pressure. Symptomatic hypotension, including orthostatic hypotension, may occur, particularly in patients taking several antihypertensive medicinal products, patients with volume depletion and elderly patients. Volume depletion should be corrected before tavorenone is started.

Patients with acute illness that causes volume depletion (e.g. vomiting, diarrhoea or reduced fluid intake) are at increased risk of hyperkalaemia and worsening of renal function. Temporary interruption of tavorenone should be considered until the condition resolves and serum potassium and eGFR have been checked.

Patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and NYHA class II–IV were excluded from TAVOLA-CKD. There are no data on the use of tavorenone in place of an established mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist in these patients.

Tavorenone has not been studied in kidney transplant recipients. Calcineurin inhibitors used in these patients (ciclosporin, tacrolimus) increase the risk of hyperkalaemia and are also CYP3A4 substrates or inhibitors (see section 4.5). Use in this population is not recommended.

Elderly patients are more likely to have reduced renal function and to take medicinal products that increase serum potassium. Serum potassium and renal function should be monitored regularly (see section 4.2).

div.p: The dose of tavorenone should not exceed 12.5 mg once daily during concomitant use with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, and serum potassium should be monitored (see sections 4.2 and 4.5).
Concomitant use of tavorenone with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inducers is not recommended (see section 4.5).
Grapefruit or grapefruit juice should not be consumed during treatment with tavorenone (see section 4.5).

Tavorenone should not be used during pregnancy unless the clinical condition of the woman requires treatment with tavorenone. Women of childbearing potential should use effective contraception during treatment with tavorenone (see sections 4.6 and 5.3).
Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
This medicinal product contains less than 1 mmol sodium (23 mg) per tablet, that is to say essentially 'sodium-free'.

title.value: 4.5 Interaction with other medicinal products and other forms of interaction

display.value: 4.5 Interaction with other medicinal products and other forms of interaction

div.p: Interaction studies have only been performed in adults.
Tavorenone is eliminated almost entirely by oxidative metabolism, mainly by CYP3A4 (about 85%) with a minor contribution from CYP2C8 (about 10%) (see section 5.2).

title.value: Effects of other medicinal products on tavorenone

div.p: Itraconazole (200 mg once daily) increased tavorenone AUC 5.8-fold and Cmax 2.3-fold. Concomitant use of tavorenone with itraconazole and other strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole, ritonavir, cobicistat, clarithromycin) is contraindicated (see section 4.3), because a marked increase in tavorenone exposure, and therefore in the risk of hyperkalaemia, is expected.

Rifampicin (600 mg once daily) decreased tavorenone AUC by 89%. Efavirenz (600 mg once daily), a moderate CYP3A4 inducer, decreased tavorenone AUC by 52% in physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations. Concomitant use of tavorenone with rifampicin and other strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St John's wort [Hypericum perforatum]) or with moderate CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. efavirenz, bosentan) is not recommended, as reduced efficacy is expected.

em.span: Potassium-sparing diuretics and other mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists

div.p: Concomitant use of tavorenone with amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone or potassium canrenoate is not recommended because of the increased risk of hyperkalaemia (see section 4.4).
Grapefruit and grapefruit juice inhibit CYP3A4 and are expected to increase tavorenone plasma concentrations. They should not be consumed during treatment (see sections 4.2 and 4.4).

Erythromycin (500 mg three times daily) increased tavorenone AUC 3.1-fold and Cmax 1.8-fold. Verapamil (240 mg prolonged-release once daily) increased tavorenone AUC 2.4-fold. In PBPK simulations, fluconazole (200 mg once daily) and diltiazem (120 mg twice daily) increased tavorenone AUC 2.2-fold and 2.0-fold, respectively. During concomitant use with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, the tavorenone dose should not exceed 12.5 mg once daily and serum potassium should be monitored (see sections 4.2 and 4.4).

Weak CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. fluvoxamine, cimetidine) increased tavorenone AUC by up to 1.5-fold in PBPK simulations. No dose adjustment is required. Serum potassium monitoring should be considered when such a medicinal product is started.
Gemfibrozil (600 mg twice daily) increased tavorenone AUC 1.2-fold. This is not considered clinically relevant.

em.span: Medicinal products that increase serum potassium

div.p: Concomitant use with potassium supplements, potassium-containing salt substitutes, trimethoprim, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, heparin, ciclosporin or tacrolimus may increase the risk of hyperkalaemia. Serum potassium should be monitored (see section 4.4).

p.em: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors

div.p: In the clinical studies, tavorenone was given in addition to an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Combining these medicinal products increases the risk of hyperkalaemia. Serum potassium should be monitored. Combining tavorenone with both an ACE inhibitor and an ARB (dual renin-angiotensin system blockade) has not been studied and is not recommended.
The blood pressure-lowering effect of tavorenone is additive to that of other antihypertensive medicinal products. Blood pressure should be monitored, especially when treatment is started.

NSAIDs, including selective COX-2 inhibitors, may reduce the antihypertensive effect of tavorenone and increase the risk of hyperkalaemia and worsening of renal function. Serum potassium and renal function should be monitored when NSAIDs are used concomitantly.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists may reduce the renal clearance of lithium. If the combination is necessary, serum lithium levels should be monitored.

title.value: Effects of tavorenone on other medicinal products

div.p: At 25 mg once daily, tavorenone had no clinically relevant effect on the pharmacokinetics of midazolam (CYP3A4 substrate), repaglinide (CYP2C8 substrate), warfarin (CYP2C9 substrate) or rosuvastatin (BCRP and OATP1B1 substrate). Tavorenone increased digoxin (P-gp substrate) AUC by 12%, which is not considered clinically relevant. No dose adjustment of these medicinal products is required.
Women of childbearing potential should use effective contraception during treatment with tavorenone and for 1 week after the last dose.
There are no data from the use of tavorenone in pregnant women. Studies in animals have shown reproductive toxicity (see section 5.3).

Kalvenzo should not be used during pregnancy unless the clinical condition of the woman requires treatment with tavorenone. If a woman becomes pregnant during treatment, she should be informed of the potential risk to the foetus.

It is unknown whether tavorenone or its metabolites are excreted in human milk. Available data in animals have shown excretion of tavorenone in milk (see section 5.3). A risk to newborns/infants cannot be excluded.
Kalvenzo should not be used during breast-feeding.

There are no data on the effect of tavorenone on human fertility. In rats, tavorenone reduced female fertility at exposures well above human exposure at the maximum recommended dose. No effects on male fertility were observed (see section 5.3).

title.value: 4.7 Effects on ability to drive and use machines

display.value: 4.7 Effects on ability to drive and use machines

div.p: Kalvenzo has minor influence on the ability to drive and use machines. Dizziness and symptomatic hypotension may occur, particularly at the start of treatment (see section 4.8). Patients should be advised not to drive or use machines if they experience these symptoms.

The most frequently reported adverse reaction with tavorenone was hyperkalaemia (13.8%). Other common adverse reactions were hypotension, dizziness, glomerular filtration rate decreased and hyponatraemia. The adverse reaction that most often led to permanent discontinuation was hyperkalaemia (1.9%).

The safety of tavorenone was evaluated in 3 833 patients treated with 12.5 mg or 25 mg once daily in the phase III studies TAVOLA-CKD (3 201 patients with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes, mean treatment duration 2.5 years) and TAVOLA-HTN (632 patients with resistant hypertension, including the open-label extension, mean treatment duration 0.9 years).

Adverse reactions are listed below by MedDRA system organ class and frequency. Frequencies are defined as: very common (≥1/10); common (≥1/100 to <1/10); uncommon (≥1/1,000 to <1/100); rare (≥1/10,000 to <1/1,000); very rare (<1/10,000); not known (cannot be estimated from the available data). Within each frequency group, adverse reactions are presented in order of decreasing seriousness.

In TAVOLA-CKD, hyperkalaemia events were reported in 13.8% of tavorenone-treated patients and 6.4% of placebo-treated patients. Serious hyperkalaemia was reported in 1.2% and 0.3%, respectively. Serum potassium > 5.5 mmol/L and > 6.0 mmol/L was observed in 17.9% and 3.6% of tavorenone-treated patients, compared with 7.8% and 1.4% of placebo-treated patients. Hyperkalaemia led to permanent discontinuation in 1.9% of tavorenone-treated patients and 0.5% of placebo-treated patients, and to hospitalisation in 1.0% and 0.2%, respectively. Mean serum potassium increased by 0.22 mmol/L relative to placebo during the first month and then remained stable. In TAVOLA-HTN, hyperkalaemia was reported in 6.1% of tavorenone-treated patients and 1.9% of placebo-treated patients. Most events were mild or moderate and resolved with dose adjustment or interruption (see sections 4.2 and 4.4).

In TAVOLA-CKD, glomerular filtration rate decreased was reported in 6.2% of tavorenone-treated patients and 4.7% of placebo-treated patients, and acute kidney injury in 0.9% and 0.8%, respectively. Patients treated with tavorenone had an initial mean decrease in eGFR of 2.6 mL/min/1.73 m² at month 1 compared with placebo. This decrease stayed stable, and the annual rate of eGFR decline after month 4 was lower with tavorenone than with placebo (see section 5.1). Events related to worsening of renal function led to permanent discontinuation in 0.4% of patients in each group.

Tavorenone lowered mean systolic blood pressure by 4 mm Hg and mean diastolic blood pressure by 2 mm Hg compared with placebo at month 1 in TAVOLA-CKD. Hypotension was reported in 5.3% of tavorenone-treated patients and 3.2% of placebo-treated patients. Tavorenone was permanently discontinued because of hypotension in 0.2% of patients.
Hyponatraemia (serum sodium < 135 mmol/L) was reported in 2.4% of tavorenone-treated patients and 1.3% of placebo-treated patients. Events were mild and none led to discontinuation.

Hyperuricaemia was reported in 4.6% of tavorenone-treated patients and 3.5% of placebo-treated patients in TAVOLA-CKD. Mean serum uric acid increased by 0.25 mg/dL relative to placebo by month 12, and the difference became smaller over time. Gout was reported in 0.9% and 0.6% of patients, respectively. No event led to permanent discontinuation.

Tavorenone was associated with a placebo-corrected decrease in mean haemoglobin of 0.12 g/dL at month 4, which did not progress. Anaemia was reported in 0.8% of tavorenone-treated patients and 0.6% of placebo-treated patients.
In contrast to steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, the incidence of gynaecomastia with tavorenone (0.05%) was similar to placebo (0.03%).

In TAVOLA-CKD, hyperkalaemia was reported in 16.2% of tavorenone-treated patients aged 75 years and older, compared with 13.1% of those under 65 years. Hypotension was reported in 7.8% and 4.4%, respectively. The overall safety profile was otherwise similar across age groups (see section 4.4).

The incidence of hyperkalaemia increased as baseline eGFR fell. It was 9.1%, 14.6% and 21.3% in tavorenone-treated patients with eGFR ≥ 60, 45 to < 60 and 25 to < 45 mL/min/1.73 m², respectively. The corresponding placebo rates were 4.0%, 6.9% and 10.2% (see sections 4.2 and 4.4).
Patients with moderate hepatic impairment were under-represented in the clinical studies (1.1%). No difference in the type of adverse reactions was identified.

Reporting suspected adverse reactions after authorisation of the medicinal product is important. It allows continued monitoring of the benefit/risk balance of the medicinal product. Healthcare professionals are asked to report any suspected adverse reactions via the national reporting system listed in Appendix V.
Single doses of up to 200 mg and multiple doses of up to 75 mg once daily for 14 days were well tolerated in healthy participants.
The most likely signs of overdose are hyperkalaemia and hypotension.

There is no specific antidote. Tavorenone should be stopped, and serum potassium, renal function and blood pressure monitored. Hyperkalaemia should be treated according to standard practice. Because of its high plasma protein binding (about 94%), tavorenone is not expected to be removed effectively by haemodialysis.
Pharmacotherapeutic group: diuretics, aldosterone antagonists, ATC code: C03DA06

Tavorenone is a nonsteroidal, highly selective antagonist of the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR). It binds the MR with high affinity (IC50 9 nM) and has more than 500-fold selectivity over the glucocorticoid, androgen and progesterone receptors. Binding of tavorenone blocks aldosterone- and cortisol-mediated MR activation in the kidney, heart and blood vessels. In the kidney this reduces sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal nephron. In non-epithelial tissues it reduces the expression of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic mediators. Because tavorenone has a nonsteroidal structure and a balanced tissue distribution between heart and kidney, it is less likely than steroidal MR antagonists to cause sex-hormone-related effects.

In TAVOLA-CKD, tavorenone reduced the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) by 34% relative to placebo at month 4 (95% CI 31%; 37%), and the reduction was maintained throughout the study. In a phase II dose-finding study (TAVOLA-DF, N = 612), placebo-corrected UACR reductions at day 90 were 18%, 29% and 37% with 5 mg, 12.5 mg and 25 mg once daily, respectively.
Plasma renin activity and serum aldosterone increased in a dose-dependent way during treatment. This reflects the expected compensatory response to MR blockade.
In a thorough QT study in 64 healthy participants, single doses of 25 mg (therapeutic) and 100 mg (supratherapeutic) tavorenone did not prolong the QTc interval.

em.span: Chronic kidney disease associated with type 2 diabetes

div.p: The efficacy of tavorenone was evaluated in TAVOLA-CKD, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven, multicentre phase III study in adults with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes. Eligible patients had a UACR of ≥ 200 to ≤ 5 000 mg/g, an eGFR of 25 to < 75 mL/min/1.73 m² and serum potassium ≤ 4.8 mmol/L at screening. All patients were receiving the maximum tolerated labelled dose of an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and New York Heart Association (NYHA) class II–IV were excluded.

The primary endpoint was a composite of time to first kidney failure (chronic dialysis, kidney transplantation or sustained eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m²), sustained decline in eGFR of ≥ 40% from baseline, or renal death. The key secondary endpoint was a composite of time to cardiovascular (CV) death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke or hospitalisation for heart failure.

A total of 6 412 patients were randomised to tavorenone (N = 3 204) or placebo (N = 3 208). The dose could be adjusted between 12.5 mg and 25 mg once daily, mainly according to serum potassium. At month 12, 71% of tavorenone-treated patients were taking 25 mg once daily, 26% were taking 12.5 mg once daily and 3% had interrupted treatment. Median follow-up was 2.8 years.

The mean age at baseline was 65 years and 68% of patients were male. The population was 66% White, 22% Asian and 6% Black. Mean eGFR was 46.1 mL/min/1.73 m², median UACR was 742 mg/g, mean HbA1c was 7.6% and mean blood pressure was 137/77 mm Hg. At baseline, 37% of patients were taking an ACE inhibitor and 63% an ARB. 21% were taking a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor and 12% a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist.

Tavorenone showed a statistically significant reduction in the primary kidney composite endpoint and the key secondary CV composite endpoint compared with placebo (table 4). The effect on the primary endpoint was consistent across prespecified subgroups, including baseline eGFR, UACR, region and SGLT2 inhibitor use at baseline.

Results were also consistent across baseline eGFR (≥ 45 versus < 45 mL/min/1.73 m²; HR 0.74 and 0.80) and baseline UACR (< 1 000 versus ≥ 1 000 mg/g; HR 0.82 and 0.75).

TAVOLA-HTN was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase III study in 842 adults with resistant hypertension. Patients had a seated systolic blood pressure (SBP) of 140 to 180 mm Hg despite at least 3 antihypertensive medicinal products, including a diuretic, at maximally tolerated doses, and an eGFR ≥ 45 mL/min/1.73 m². Patients were randomised 3:1 to tavorenone (12.5 mg once daily, increased to 25 mg at week 4 if serum potassium ≤ 5.0 mmol/L; N = 632) or placebo (N = 210) for 12 weeks. Mean age was 62 years, 57% of patients were male and mean baseline seated SBP was 152.6 mm Hg.

The primary endpoint was the change from baseline in mean seated office SBP at week 12. Tavorenone reduced seated SBP by 12.4 mm Hg compared with 4.1 mm Hg with placebo (placebo-corrected difference −8.3 mm Hg; 95% CI −10.2; −6.4; p < 0.001; table 5). At week 12, 81% of tavorenone-treated patients were taking 25 mg once daily. The effect was maintained over 40 weeks in the open-label extension (mean change from baseline at week 52: −13.0 mm Hg).

Tavorenone is rapidly and almost completely absorbed after oral administration. Maximum plasma concentrations (Cmax) are reached 1.5 to 2.5 hours after dosing. Absolute bioavailability is 62% because of first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver. Steady state is reached by day 3 of once-daily dosing, with an accumulation ratio of about 1.3.

A high-fat, high-calorie meal increased tavorenone AUC by 18%, reduced Cmax by 15% and delayed tmax by about 1 hour. These changes are not clinically relevant, and tavorenone can be taken with or without food. Crushing the 25 mg tablet and mixing it with apple sauce did not change exposure.
The volume of distribution at steady state (Vss) is about 74 L. Plasma protein binding is about 94%, mainly to albumin, and does not depend on concentration. The blood-to-plasma ratio is 0.71.

Tavorenone is extensively metabolised, about 85% by CYP3A4 and about 10% by CYP2C8. There is a minor contribution from glucuronidation by UGT1A3. The two main circulating metabolites, M1 (hydroxylated) and M2 (N-dealkylated), account for 32% and 18% of total drug-related exposure. Both are pharmacologically inactive at the mineralocorticoid receptor.

In vitro, tavorenone does not inhibit or induce the main CYP enzymes at clinically relevant concentrations, and does not inhibit OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1 or MATE2-K. It is a weak in vitro inhibitor of P-gp (see section 4.5).

Tavorenone has a terminal elimination half-life (t½) of 9 to 11 hours, and an apparent oral clearance (CL/F) of about 6.2 L/h. After a single oral dose of radiolabelled tavorenone, 68% of radioactivity was recovered in urine and 29% in faeces, almost entirely as metabolites. Less than 1% of the dose was excreted unchanged in urine.
Tavorenone pharmacokinetics are linear and dose-proportional across single doses of 2.5 to 100 mg and multiple doses of 5 to 75 mg once daily. They do not change over time.

In population pharmacokinetic analyses, AUC was about 19% higher in patients aged 75 years and older than in patients under 65 years. This is not clinically relevant, and no dose adjustment is required (see section 4.2). In TAVOLA-CKD, 55% of tavorenone-treated patients were 65 years or older and 13% were 75 years or older.

Compared with participants with normal renal function (creatinine clearance [CLCR] ≥ 90 mL/min), tavorenone AUC was 11% higher in mild (CLCR 60 to < 90 mL/min), 28% higher in moderate (CLCR 30 to < 60 mL/min) and 45% higher in severe (CLCR < 30 mL/min) renal impairment. Cmax was not affected. Because of high protein binding, tavorenone is not expected to be removed by dialysis (see section 4.2).

Compared with healthy participants, total tavorenone AUC was 14% higher in mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh A) and 62% higher in moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B). Unbound AUC was 85% higher in moderate hepatic impairment. Patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) have not been studied (see sections 4.2 and 4.3).

Population pharmacokinetic analyses found no clinically relevant effect of sex or race on tavorenone exposure. AUC was about 25% higher in patients weighing under 60 kg and about 20% lower in patients weighing over 120 kg than in patients weighing 60 to 120 kg. No dose adjustment is required (see section 4.2).

The reduction in UACR followed an Emax relationship with tavorenone exposure and was close to maximal at the exposure reached with 25 mg once daily. Mean serum potassium increased with exposure. This relationship is the basis for the potassium-guided dose titration in section 4.2. The full effect on UACR developed over about 3 to 4 months, much more slowly than the pharmacokinetic half-life would suggest. This is consistent with an indirect mechanism.
Non-clinical data reveal no special hazard for humans based on conventional studies of safety pharmacology, genotoxicity and male fertility.

In 26-week rat and 39-week dog studies, the main findings were consistent with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism: increased serum potassium, decreased serum sodium and hypertrophy of the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex. These occurred at unbound exposures (AUCunbound) 3 to 5 times human exposure at 25 mg. In dogs, reversible reductions in prostate weight were seen at about 12 times human AUCunbound.

In 2-year studies, tavorenone was not carcinogenic in female rats or in mice of either sex. In male rats, the incidence of benign adrenal cortical adenoma increased at about 18 times human AUCunbound. This is considered a rodent-specific result of chronic MR blockade and of the secondary rise in aldosterone, and is not relevant to humans. Exposures of 7 times human AUCunbound caused no tumours.

In rats, tavorenone reduced the number of corpora lutea and implantation sites, and increased pre-implantation loss, at 14 times human AUCunbound. No effect on female fertility was seen at 5 times human AUCunbound. Male fertility was not affected at up to 22 times human AUCunbound.

In the embryo-foetal development study in rats, reduced foetal weight and delayed ossification were seen at maternally toxic doses (about 9 times human AUCunbound). At 20 times human AUCunbound, an increase in skeletal variations and one case of ventricular septal defect were observed. There were no findings in rabbits up to 11 times human AUCunbound.

In the pre- and postnatal development study in rats, pup survival and body weight gain were reduced at about 4 times human AUCunbound. Radiolabelled tavorenone was transferred into the milk of lactating rats, where concentrations were about 1.6 times those in maternal plasma (see section 4.6).
Tavorenone is not readily biodegradable. Environmental risk assessment studies indicate that it may pose a risk to the aquatic compartment (see section 6.6).
